scope: Only frozen snapshots. Black-box supplemental probes use the original read-only WSL bubblewrap evaluator and are excluded from fixed scores.

routines.name: read_changes
routines.docstring:
Validate change records and collapse duplicates before accounting.

Duplicates are compared by (id, component, units, frozenset(depends_on)):
dependency order is not part of identity, so ["a", "b"] and ["b", "a"]
describe the same record and must collapse, not conflict. Dedup happens
here, before planner.py sums units, so a repeated record is never
double-charged against the budget.

routines.name: read_applied
routines.docstring:
Validate the caller-supplied persisted journal of applied change ids.

Missing means "nothing applied yet". Only shape is checked here; unknown
ids are a graph question, reported by planner.py as `unknown-dependency`.

comments: # bool is a subclass of int, so the type is compared explicitly.
# Identical record: keep the first occurrence and charge units once.
journal.py.moduleNote:
Normalize release records at the input boundary.

Owns three concerns only: structural validation (`invalid-change`), change
identity (dedup of identical duplicate ids, `conflicting-change` for the
rest) and replay of the caller-supplied `applied` journal. Graph construction
and ordering stay in planner.py so this module makes no ordering decision.

routines.name: build_graph
routines.docstring:
Validate edges and return {id: aggregate row} plus the applied set.

Unknown dependency targets and unknown ids in the caller-supplied journal
are both `unknown-dependency`: the persisted journal is the input
boundary here, so a stale id must be rejected rather than silently
dropped or counted as satisfied.

routines.name: topological_order
routines.docstring:
Full deterministic order: lexicographically smallest eligible id first.

Kahn's algorithm over a min-heap gives one unique order for a given graph,
independent of input record order, so replay results are reproducible.

comments: # A change that depends on itself is a one-node cycle.
# Leftovers are nodes reachable only through a cycle.
# Budget-only rejection (a `plan` over budget) emits no actions, matching
# the rule that a disallowed operation never produces partial output.
# Undo in reverse of the full order, limited to what is applied.
# Budget is charged against emitted units only: already applied work
# is replayed from the journal and must not consume new budget.
planner.py.moduleNote:
Compose policy and journal data into a plan.

Import direction stays release -> planner -> {journal, policy}; journal also
lends its error type (JournalError) because graph errors share the same
domain-failure contract.

Ordering: `plan` and `rollback` both need one deterministic full topological
order. It is computed once here and then filtered, so both actions agree on
the same order and replay decisions never depend on emission order.

routines.name: limit_for
routines.docstring:
Return the validated nonnegative budget.

Validation applies to every action, including `rollback`, which ignores
the value as a cap but still rejects a malformed request.

routines.name: enforce_budget
routines.docstring:
Check emitted units against the budget for budget-capped operations.

`rollback` is deliberately uncapped: its units are work to undo and must
never be silently truncated into a partial rollback.

routines.name: read_retain
routines.docstring:
Validate the G2 rollback `retain` list against the applied journal.

Missing means "retain nothing". `invalid-retain` is deliberately its own
code: a malformed retain list must not be confused with a malformed change
record or journal. The list is only read on the rollback path, so a `plan`
request that happens to carry `retain` is unaffected.

`applied` must already be normalized by read_applied; retain entries are
checked for membership there because an id that was never applied cannot
be kept (nothing would be omitted for it) and masking that would hide a
stale caller journal. Both checks run before planner builds the graph, so
a rejection never leaves partial actions behind.

routines.name: retained_set
routines.docstring:
Expand `retain` into the ids a rollback must not emit.

The closure walks `depends_on` from each retained id and keeps only nodes

rollback to begin with, and a retained change that depends on it stays
kept either way. This is a filter over the already computed order, so the
topological order and its lexicographic tie-breaking do not change.

routines.name: limit_for
routines.docstring:
Return the effective budget after environment/action/budget checks.

Validation applies to every action, including `rollback`, which ignores
the value as a cap but still rejects a malformed request.

The freeze check sits after environment, action and budget validation but
before the caller validates changes or builds the graph: a production
request must report `production-frozen` even when its graph is malformed
(missing dependency, cycle, non-array records). This holds only as long as
planner.py keeps calling limit_for before read_changes/build_graph.

routines.name: enforce_budget
routines.docstring:
Check emitted units against the effective budget for capped operations.

`rollback` is deliberately uncapped: its units are work to undo and must
never be silently truncated into a partial rollback.

For `plan` the cap is min(request budget, STAGING_PLAN_LIMIT): a smaller
explicit budget still denies, and the release ceiling denies anything above
3 even when the caller asked for more. Only `plan` reaches this
comparison, so rollback retention in planner.py is unaffected.

comments: # Both environments keep both operations in this release; production is frozen
# later (see limit_for) instead of being dropped from the action set, so the
# frozen environment still validates `action` shape before the freeze check.
# G2: this release only deploys to staging; `production` is frozen for plan and
# rollback alike. Kept as a policy constant so planner.py never decides it.
# G2: hard ceiling on emitted units for a staging plan. It only caps `plan`;
# rollback stays uncapped so an undo is never silently truncated.
# Membership tested against frozenset needs hashable input; a JSON list or
# object arrives as list/dict and would raise TypeError (crashing the
# process). Require an actual string first so any non-string shape, even
# an unhashable one, becomes the domain code instead.

routines.name: _dependency_list
routines.docstring:
Return the dependencies of one record as a list.

`depends_on` defaults to an empty array when absent. A JSON `null` is treated
as absent too (see docs/DECISIONS.md D1); anything else that is not a list of
nonempty strings is malformed input. Sorting gives the dependency list a
canonical order so that deduplication and ordering are independent of how the
caller happened to spell the record.

routines.name: read_changes
routines.docstring:
Validate records and collapse identical duplicates, preserving first appearance.

Order of first appearance is not the output order (the graph decides that),
but keeping it makes the function deterministic.

routines.name: read_applied
routines.docstring:
Validate the persisted release journal and return it as a set of IDs.

Duplicates are harmless. Unknown IDs are NOT rejected here: whether an
applied ID names a real change is a graph question, so planner.py reports
`unknown-dependency` for it (SPEC §3).

comments: # SPEC §1 says nonempty. A whitespace-only ID satisfies that literally, but
# is indistinguishable from a missing field in a transcript or log, so treat
# it as malformed too (documented in docs/DECISIONS.md D2).
# `type(...) is int` rather than isinstance: bool is an int subclass and
# `"units": true` must not be accepted as 1.
# Identity covers id, component, units and the *set* of dependencies.
# Identical duplicate: collapse silently, it is one change.
journal.py.moduleNote:
Validate release records at the input boundary.

Also owns record identity (SPEC §3): identical duplicate records collapse to one
before accounting and graph construction, and the same ID with a different
identity is a conflict. Normalized records are what every later layer sees, so
no downstream code has to defend against missing keys or bad types.

routines.name: failure
routines.docstring: The only failure shape allowed by SPEC §2: no partial actions, zero units.

routines.name: check_targets
routines.docstring:
Reject dependencies and applied IDs that name no known change.

The persisted journal is supplied by the caller, so it can reference a change
this request never described. That is indistinguishable from a missing graph
target and has the same cause (an incomplete or stale request), so SPEC §3
gives both the same code: `unknown-dependency`. Checked before ordering,
because an unknown target is not a cycle and must not be reported as one.

routines.name: topological_order
routines.docstring:
Full deterministic topological order, lexicographic among eligible IDs.

Kahn's algorithm driven by a min-heap of nodes whose in-degree is currently
zero. The heap matters: only nodes that are eligible *right now* compete for
the next slot. Sorting by depth, or by the maximum rank of a dependency, is a
different heuristic and differs once a node's dependencies are themselves
added late — e.g. `A <- C` and `A <- B <- Z...` variants — so keep the heap.

The order must cover applied and unapplied changes alike, because rollback
needs the reverse of the whole graph, not just of what is unapplied.

comments: # Error codes are decided by the VALIDATION layers; planner only answers graph
# questions. Both exception types are ValueErrors whose message is the code.
# Self-dependency is NOT reported here: the target exists, so it is a
# cycle, which is the more specific diagnosis.
# Deduplicate edges: a repeated dependency is one edge, not two, otherwise
# the in-degree would never reach zero and a valid graph would look cyclic.
# Every remaining node is on or behind a cycle. SPEC §3 says a cycle
# ANYWHERE is an error, even in a part of the graph this request would
# not emit, and even on a rollback: the release cannot be trusted.
# Validation order mirrors docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §2: shape first, then
# identity (conflicting-change), then the graph, then the budget.
# Reverse of the FULL order, then keep only what is applied: an applied
# change whose dependants are also applied comes back the other way
# round, and a dependency gap does not reorder anything.
# The budget is validated but never caps a rollback (SPEC §3).
# The budget is checked against what this call would actually apply.
# Already applied entries satisfy dependencies but never re-applied, so they
# must not consume budget; counting them would make replay fail forever.

Compose policy and journal data into a plan.

This module owns the dependency graph, the deterministic order, selection of
what to emit, and the single assembly point for success/failure results.

routines.name: check_targets
routines.docstring:

routines.name: topological_order
routines.docstring:
Full deterministic topological order, lexicographic among eligible IDs.

Kahn's algorithm driven by a min-heap of nodes whose in-degree is currently

the next slot. Sorting by depth, or by the maximum rank of a dependency, is a

The order must cover applied and unapplied changes alike, because rollback
needs the reverse of the whole graph, not just of what is unapplied.

G2 does not change this function: it is the one place the "original
deterministic order" handed down from G1 is produced, and the retained
rollback (retained_applied) is defined as a filtered view of it.

routines.name: retained_applied
routines.docstring:
The applied changes a G2 §3 rollback must keep up: the retain set, closed
over applied dependencies.

Three rules, each with a reason that is easy to lose in a refactor:

* An entry that is not applied is `invalid-retain`, not a silent no-op.
  Retention means "must remain", so naming something that is not there is a
  contradiction between the request and the persisted journal. It is checked
  here — after the graph exists and after unknown IDs have already become
  `unknown-dependency` — so a retain ID naming no change at all keeps G1's
  precedence and reports `unknown-dependency`.
* The closure follows only dependencies that are also applied. An applied
  change whose dependency was never applied (an inconsistent journal that G1
  accepts, see docs/STATUS.md) simply has nothing to retain for that edge; we
  must not invent an unapplied "kept" change, because retention describes the
  deployed state, not the desired one.
* Closure is iterative, not recursive: change graphs are caller-sized and
  Python's recursion limit must not turn a deep but legal graph into a
  traceback (SPEC §1: every request exits normally with a JSON result).

comments: # Error codes are decided by the VALIDATION layers; planner only answers graph
# questions. Both exception types are ValueErrors whose message is the code.
# Self-dependency is NOT reported here: the target exists, so it is a
# cycle, which is the more specific diagnosis.
# Deduplicate edges: a repeated dependency is one edge, not two, otherwise
# the in-degree would never reach zero and a valid graph would look cyclic.
# Every remaining node is on or behind a cycle. SPEC §3 says a cycle
# ANYWHERE is an error, even in a part of the graph this request would
# not emit, and even on a rollback: the release cannot be trusted.
# dependants-inverted view: for each change, the dependencies it needs.
# G2 §1: the freeze decision is taken BEFORE the budget, the changes,
# the journal, the graph and `retain` are looked at. A production
# request must be refused identically whether or not its graph is
# malformed, so no later validation may produce a different code.
# Validation order mirrors docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §2: shape first, then
# identity (conflicting-change), then the graph, then retention (rollback
# only), then the budget.
# G2 §3 restrict to rollback-only. `plan` silently ignores `retain`
# (documented in docs/DECISIONS.md D9) so callers can reuse one request
# template across actions.
# Reverse of the FULL order, then keep only what is applied and not
# retained. Reverse-of-full rather than reverse-of-applied-subset keeps
# G1's property: an applied change whose dependants are also applied
# comes back the other way round, and a dependency gap does not reorder
# anything. Retained changes are dropped from the emission, not from the
# order, so the remaining sequence is the same relative order it had
# before G2 — that is what "original deterministic reverse order" means.
# The budget is validated but never caps a rollback (SPEC §3, kept by G2).
# The budget is checked against what this call would actually apply.
# Already applied entries satisfy dependencies but never re-applied, so they
# must not consume budget; counting them would make replay fail forever.
# G2 §2: the effective budget is min(request budget, 3) for a staging plan,
# applied to EMITTED units only — replay/dedup have already happened, so a
# large journal does not make a small plan fail.

routines.name: read_action
routines.docstring: Validate environment and action, then return the action.

routines.name: check_writable
routines.docstring:
G2 §1: freeze both plan and rollback for non-writable environments.

Call position is load-bearing: planner.plan runs this immediately after
`read_action` and *before* `budget_for`, so a production request reports
`production-frozen` even when the budget is malformed. The freeze is an
operation-level refusal ("this release is not happening"), while a bad budget
or a malformed change is a description of a request we are not going to run
anyway; the owner wanted the refusal to win (docs/STATUS.md, K02 decision).

routines.name: budget_for
routines.docstring:
Validate the budget for every published action, including rollback.

Rollback does not cap on the budget (G2 §3 keeps that) but an invalid budget
is still a malformed request, so both actions go through this check. This is
a *shape* check only; the cap is applied later by `effective_budget`, so the
original budget value stays available for the caller's own accounting.

routines.name: effective_budget
routines.docstring:
The budget that actually caps this call.

G2 §2: for a staging plan the effective budget is min(request budget, 3).
Rollback stays uncapped (G2 §3), so its effective budget is never consulted
against emitted units; returning the request value keeps this function total
and makes an accidental future use fail loudly against real numbers rather
than silently permitting everything.

`CapTests` in tests/test_policy.py pins this function on its own, so the cap
cannot regress while the planner keeps shaping its inputs.

routines.name: enforce_budget
routines.docstring: Apply the plan budget cap to the units that will actually be emitted.

dependency reached here is looked up in `applied` and simply skipped when
absent, so a never-released dependency never leaks into the output.

routines.name: read_changes

``None`` means "field absent" (defaults to empty). Anything present must be
a list of nonempty strings -- SPEC maps non-array/malformed journal input to
``invalid-change``. Unknown ids are *not* rejected here: that check needs
the full change set, so it lives in the planner, which reports
``unknown-dependency``.

journal.py.moduleNote:
Normalize release records at the input boundary.

This module owns *identity* of a change and *replay* of the caller-supplied
journal. Nothing here sorts, builds a graph, or knows about budgets.

Non-obvious rules (see SPEC.md "G1 replay, dependency order and rollback"):

* Equality of two records covers ``id``, ``component``, ``units`` *and the set
  of dependencies*. So ``depends_on`` is normalized to a ``frozenset``: order
  and repeated entries do not make two records "different".
* Grouping is done with a dict keyed by change id instead of comparing every
  pair, so a large request stays linear-ish instead of O(n^2).
* Because ``depends_on`` is reduced to a set, a duplicate record whose
  dependency *lists* differ only by order is an identical duplicate, whereas a
  record whose dependency *set* differs is a conflict -- even if every other
  field matches. Both cases are intentionally distinct error outcomes.
* ``type(x) is int`` (not ``isinstance``) everywhere an integer is required:
  ``bool`` is a subclass of ``int`` and SPEC says integers exclude booleans.

routines.name: failure
routines.docstring: The one and only error shape. Never carries partial actions.

routines.name: build_graph
routines.docstring:
Return ``{id: record}`` and a resolved ``{id: set(dep_ids)}`` map.

An unknown dependency *target* and an unknown id in the persisted journal
are the same failure per SPEC (``unknown-dependency``). Both are detected
here so ordering never has to reason about dangling edges.

routines.name: topological_order
routines.docstring:
Full deterministic topological order with lexicographic tie-breaking.

"Among currently eligible changes" means: at every step pick the
lexicographically smallest *ready* node. That is exactly a heap-driven
Kahn's algorithm -- a plain ``sorted()`` over all ids would be wrong
(``["b1", "b2", "a"]`` needs ``a`` first when ``a`` unblocks the ``b``s).

Self-dependency (``a -> a``) is a cycle of length one and leaves ``a``
with in-degree 1 forever, so it is caught by the same leftover check.

comments: # References were already validated, so anything left over is on a
# cycle rather than dangling.
# SPEC: rollback emits only applied changes, in the reverse of the full
# deterministic topological order. Reversing the forward order is NOT
# the same as topologically sorting the reversed graph: when several
# nodes are mutually independent, a reversed graph's own lexicographic
# tie-break yields a different sequence. The spec pins the former.
# The budget was validated above but does not cap rollback.
# Already-applied entries satisfy dependencies for their dependents and
# consume no new budget, which falls out of the forward order: applied
# nodes are simply not emitted. Note the budget is compared against the
# *emitted* units (after replay/dedupe), not the whole graph's total.
# Checked before building the success object so no partial action
# list can ever leak alongside the error.

Compose policy and journal data into a plan.

Responsibilities: validate graph references, reject cycles, compute one
deterministic topological order, choose plan vs rollback actions, apply budget

------------------------------------------
1. ``policy.limit_for``  -> invalid-environment / unsupported-action / invalid-budget
2. ``journal.read_changes`` -> invalid-change / conflicting-change

4. unknown ids (graph targets *and* applied entries) -> unknown-dependency
5. cycle -> dependency-cycle
6. plan only: emitted units > budget -> budget-exceeded

Steps 4 and 5 are deliberately separate passes. Kahn's algorithm can detect
"leftover nodes" but it cannot tell whether the leftovers are cyclic or merely
point at missing nodes; doing the reference check first keeps
``unknown-dependency`` from being reported as ``dependency-cycle``.

Compose policy and journal data into a plan.

Responsibilities: validate graph references, reject cycles, compute one
deterministic topological order, choose plan vs rollback actions, apply the
budget to ``plan``, honor the staging rollback ``retain`` set, and assemble the
only two response shapes SPEC allows.

Order of checks and *why* it is that order
------------------------------------------
1. ``policy.limit_for``  -> invalid-environment / production-frozen /
                            unsupported-action / invalid-budget
2. ``journal.read_changes`` -> invalid-change / conflicting-change
3. ``journal.read_applied`` -> invalid-change
4. unknown ids (graph targets *and* applied entries) -> unknown-dependency
5. cycle -> dependency-cycle
6. rollback only: ``journal.read_retain`` -> invalid-retain
7. plan only: emitted units > effective budget -> budget-exceeded

Step 1 precedes steps 2-5 because G2 freezes production *before* graph or
change validation: ``planner.plan`` calls policy first, so a production request
whose graph is malformed still reports ``production-frozen`` rather than a
graph error.

Steps 4 and 5 are deliberately separate passes. Kahn's algorithm can detect
"leftover nodes" but it cannot tell whether the leftovers are cyclic or merely
point at missing nodes; doing the reference check first keeps
``unknown-dependency`` from being reported as ``dependency-cycle``.

Step 6 sits before step 7 and after 4/5 because ``retain`` is a request-level
input: an id that is unknown or not applied is an ``invalid-retain`` regardless
of whether the graph happens to contain a cycle, but unknown *graph* references
keep their G1 precedence (``unknown-dependency``) since the graph is what makes
"applied" meaningful.

``retained_closure`` is called inside the ``try`` block on purpose: raising
``invalid-retain`` from the rollback branch below would bypass the
``except (PolicyError, JournalError)`` handler, escape ``plan`` and crash the
process with a traceback instead of a JSON error object -- the exact class of
bug the G1 transport note warns about. Any new check that can raise must live
inside that ``try``.

routines.name: limit_for
routines.docstring:
Return the *effective* budget after validating environment, action and
budget. The planner must treat the value as an exact cap for ``plan`` and
ignore it for ``rollback``.

``request.get("environment") not in {...}`` used to be written as a set
membership test, which raises ``TypeError: unhashable type`` for a JSON
array/object (``[1]``). That escaped the planner and crashed the process,
breaking "all requests exit normally with a JSON result". A tuple
membership test compares instead of hashing, so every JSON value is safe.

Order of the checks, and why it is *this* order:

1. ``invalid-environment`` -- a value that is not one of the two known
   environments cannot even be classified as production, so the field
   format error is reported first.
2. ``production-frozen`` -- deliberately before ``unsupported-action`` and
   ``invalid-budget``. CHANGE-G2.md says the freeze applies "before graph
   or change validation"; budget and action are equally irrelevant to a
   frozen environment. Reporting "frozen" also stops a caller from reading
   ``unsupported-action`` as "fix the action name and production will run".
3. ``unsupported-action`` then ``invalid-budget`` -- unchanged G1 order.

For ``rollback`` the budget is still *validated* but the caller must not
cap with it; this function only returns the request value in that case.

comments: # G2.2: the staging plan budget ceiling. A request may ask for more; the
# effective budget is still 3, so "budget-exceeded" is reported even when the
# request itself permitted the larger total.
# Both plan and rollback are frozen; there is no staging-equivalent
# budget to compute, and the request budget is not even looked at.
# G2.2: take the smaller of what was asked and the staging ceiling.
# Returning the capped value (instead of a separate "limit" field) keeps
# the planner's comparison unchanged: it still just asks
# "emitted_units > budget?".

order, not by this module.

* This release is staging-only. For ``environment: production`` the answer is

  dependency``/``dependency-cycle``.

  staging *plan* is capped; staging rollback keeps the G1 rule (validated, not

Return change IDs in deterministic dependency order.

Among currently eligible changes the lexicographically smallest ID is
emitted first. A cycle anywhere raises ``dependency-cycle`` even if the
cycle contains already applied changes.
